summary.text: The Ekitiparapo (“Ekiti united”) was the alliance of the Ekiti, Ijesa, Akoko, Igbomina and Yagba kingdoms, formed in 1878 to throw off Ibadan's ajele. Its army, armed with breech-loading rifles bought through Lagos and led by the Ijesa warrior Ogedengbe, held Ibadan to a standstill at Kiriji for eight years, until a British-brokered treaty in 1886. Where Ibadan wanted one Yoruba state, the confederacy stood for a league of free kingdoms, and it preserved them to this day.

ruler.title: A council of kings and war leaders (no single ruler)

snapshots.title: The alliance forms
snapshots.text: Insulted by an Ibadan ajele, Prince Fabunmi of Okemesi kills him and calls the east to rise. The Ekiti, Ijesa, Akoko, Igbomina and Yagba form the Ekitiparapo; with Ilorin and Ila they besiege Ikirun, but Ibadan breaks the siege at Jalumi in November 1878.

links.label: Siege of Ikirun; defeat at Jalumi

snapshots.title: The Kiriji war
snapshots.text: Ogedengbe of Ilesa, twice captured by Ibadan and twice escaped, gives up a journey to Benin to command; Fabunmi stands aside for him. He had attacked Idoani in 1878. The two armies dig in facing each other at Kiriji, near Imesi-Ile, where the crack of the Ekitiparapo's breech-loaders gives the war its name.

snapshots.title: Peace treaty
snapshots.text: On 23 September 1886 the British broker peace and both camps are to break up. Ogedengbe withdraws to Imesi; when his men raid farms in 1894 Captain Bower arrests him, and the Owa of Ilesa pays £6,000 for his release. In 1898 he becomes the Obanla of Ilesa, refusing the crown itself.

today.text: The alliance ended with British rule. Its member kingdoms continue under their own Obas, such as the Owa Obokun of Ijeshaland and the Ewi of Ado-Ekiti; the Kiriji war is still commemorated.
